images.alt: Oil painting of a cosy farmhouse room with a tall clock and a curtained bed alcove. A smiling young woman in a white cap and apron holds a counter as she plays draughts against a young man in red breeches, who sits on a bench scratching his head over the board. Another young man holding a pipe leans in to watch, and an older woman looks on from behind.
images.caption: Das Damespiel (The Game of Draughts): a game at home, painted by Otto Kirberg in 1882
images.credit: Otto Kirberg, 1882. Private collection (sold by Van Ham Kunstauktionen), via Wikimedia Commons
images.note: Signed Otto Kirberg Dsdf (Düsseldorf) 1882. The people are not identified, so the caption does not claim they are one family. A young man in the picture holds a pipe.

images.alt: Colour advertising card showing four children indoors on a green rug: a boy in a white shirt with a big yellow bow and a girl in a pinafore sit on wooden stools playing draughts on a board held between them, a small girl sits on the floor watching, and a taller girl holding a doll stands at the right. The words McLaughlin's XXXX Coffee are printed along the bottom.
images.caption: Children playing draughts on a coffee company's advertising card, printed in the United States in 1892
images.credit: Cosack & Co., Buffalo and Chicago, for McLaughlin's Coffee, 1892. Cooper Hewitt, Smithsonian Design Museum, via Wikimedia Commons

images.alt: Black-and-white photograph of boys sitting on a city footpath playing draughts with round counters on the pavement, while other children in caps and shirtsleeves crowd round to watch.
images.caption: Boys playing draughts on the footpath, New York City, between 1908 and 1915
images.credit: Bain News Service, 1908 to 1915. Library of Congress, via Wikimedia Commons
images.note: Hero is 1246 px wide (Commons original 1536 px was rate-limited; the 1280 px thumbnail was used).

images.alt: Black-and-white photograph of about sixty schoolchildren and their teachers standing in rows on the verandah of a wooden schoolhouse with a shingled roof. The youngest sit in front behind a long board painted Springsure, May 1884, and a young woman in the back row holds a baby.
images.caption: Pupils and teachers on the verandah of the first Springsure State School, Queensland, May 1884
images.credit: Unknown photographer, 1884. John Oxley Library, State Library of Queensland, via Wikimedia Commons
images.note: Only a 1000 px wide copy is on Commons (the State Library of Queensland site is blocked from this network), so the hero is 950 x 722 px. A larger copy from SLQ (record 112612) would be worth fetching later.

images.alt: Black-and-white photograph of about forty children with a male and a female teacher, posed in rows on the grass in front of a weatherboard schoolhouse with a verandah and a white picket fence. A girl in the middle holds up a slate with the school's name chalked on it, and another girl in the front row holds a doll.
images.caption: Pupils and teachers outside Kettering State School, Tasmania, 1896
images.credit: Unknown photographer, 1896. Libraries Tasmania, via Wikimedia Commons

images.alt: Black-and-white street photograph of a man in a felt hat carrying a big leather-covered case on his back, with a monkey in a striped jacket and cap perched on top of it, held on a chain. Girls in wide straw hats stand beside him and a boy in a checked cap and braces watches from the right, with weatherboard houses behind.
images.caption: Children gather round a man with a monkey dressed in a cap and jacket, Tasmania, about 1900
images.credit: Unknown photographer, about 1900. Tasmanian Archive and Heritage Office (Libraries Tasmania, NS1013-1-1269), via Wikimedia Commons
images.note: Dated only c1900 by the archive, so it may fall just before Federation. Commons files it under Hobart, but the archive title does not name the place, so the caption says Tasmania. Alternative if a firmly 1901-1909 image is preferred: Six children on skis, Kiandra, NSW, probably 1906, by Charles Kerry (National Library of Australia, 1024 px): https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Six_children_on_skis,_Kiandra,_New_South_Wales,_probably_1906_-_(9287590753).jpg

images.alt: Black-and-white photograph of hundreds of schoolboys in dark suits and straw boater hats standing in rows in a large asphalt playground, all raising their arms above their heads in a drill exercise. Wooden school buildings stand on the left and a brick building with arched windows on the right.
images.caption: Senior boys doing drill in the playground at Fort Street School, Sydney, August 1913
images.credit: NSW Government Printing Office, 1913. State Records NSW (NRS 4481), via Wikimedia Commons
images.note: Source scan is 1354 px wide, so the hero is 1228 px wide after trimming the glass-plate edges.

images.alt: Colour cartoon of a white-haired man in a dark suit perched on a stool, holding his forehead as he works a sliding puzzle in a big wooden box marked The Boss Puzzle. Each numbered square has a politician's head poking up through it, labelled with names such as Grant, Blaine, Sherman and Tilden, and one square is empty.
images.caption: The Great Presidential Puzzle: a cartoon in Puck magazine, New York, March 1880, when the Fifteen Puzzle craze was at its height
images.credit: James Albert Wales, 1880 (lithograph by Mayer, Merkel & Ottmann for Puck). Library of Congress, via Wikimedia Commons

images.alt: Worn red-and-cream Victorian book cover with a chequered border and game pieces in the corners. The lettering reads Handbook of Reversi and other new games of skill: Invasion, Halma, Fanarona. Explanations, rules, problems and suggestions to players. Price 1/-. Published by F. H. Ayres, London.
images.caption: The Handbook of Reversi and other new games of skill, sold for one shilling by F. H. Ayres, London, 1889
images.credit: F. H. Ayres, London, 1889 (date from the title page). Internet Archive

images.alt: Black-and-white engraved advertisement showing three smiling children with their arms around each other above the words We are all so happy. Large lettering below reads The Popular Game Halma, E. I. Horsman, Publisher, 80 and 82 William St. N.Y.
images.caption: An advertisement for The Popular Game Halma, published by E. I. Horsman of New York, in The Century magazine, 1890
images.credit: E. I. Horsman, 1890. The Century Illustrated Monthly Magazine, via Wikimedia Commons

images.alt: Colourful box lid lettered The Popular Game of Tiddledy Winks, New Edition 1897, Parker Brothers, Salem, Mass. A family gathers round a green table: a boy flicks a coloured counter towards a small cup while his father, mother and sister watch.
images.caption: Box lid for The Popular Game of Tiddledy Winks, an 1897 edition made in Salem, Massachusetts
images.credit: Parker Brothers, 1897. Miami University Libraries, via Wikimedia Commons

images.alt: Page from an 1889 French science magazine headed Nouveaux jeux scientifiques de M. Édouard Lucas, with two engravings of peg boards. On the left, La Fasioulette, a board criss-crossed with bars. On the right, La Pipopipette: a dark board with a square grid of pegs, where white bars hooked between neighbouring pegs close off small squares. Above each board is a close-up of a peg.
images.caption: La Pipopipette, Édouard Lucas's dots-and-boxes board (right), in the French science magazine La Nature, 5 October 1889
images.credit: Engraving signed Poyet, La Nature no. 853, 5 October 1889, p. 301. Source gallica.bnf.fr / Bibliothèque nationale de France
images.note: Not on Wikimedia Commons; downloaded from Gallica's IIIF server. The 1889 engraving is public domain, but the BnF's Gallica terms ask for the credit Source gallica.bnf.fr / BnF and say non-commercial reuse is free while commercial reuse of their scans needs a licence. Fine for a free, non-commercial site; flag it if that ever changes. Gallica catalogues La Nature under its later title, Science progrès découverte.

images.alt: Colour cartoon of Uncle Sam, with untidy white hair, a blue coat and striped trousers, slumped in a green armchair and holding his head as he stares at a round Pigs in Clover puzzle in his hand. A Fifteen Puzzle box lies on the floor beside him. The caption reads: The Pigs In Clover and Fifteen Puzzle were the next Crazes that he succumbed to.
images.caption: Uncle Sam baffled by the Pigs in Clover puzzle, with a Fifteen Puzzle at his feet: one panel of a Puck cartoon about American crazes, 1896
images.credit: Frederick Burr Opper, 1896 (detail of Uncle Sam's Crazes, Past and Present, Puck). Library of Congress, via Wikimedia Commons
images.note: Cropped to panel 4 of an 1896 cartoon looking back at earlier crazes, so it is not an 1889 image. The 1889 Judge political cartoon was not found as a separate image: Commons has 1889 Judge issues only as whole-issue PDFs (for example File:JudgeMagazine27Apr1889.pdf, which is also categorised under racist caricatures and would need careful checking), and the PDF download was rate-limited. The 1889 patent drawing (File:Crandall_Pigs_in_Clover.jpg) is only 294 x 496 px.

images.alt: Watercolour of four men in turbans and white cloth sitting on the ground around a red cross-shaped cloth board with dark playing pieces on it. A bearded man on the right reaches out to move a piece, with a few small white shells by his hand, while an older man holding a long stick sits on the left. A faint handwritten pencil note runs along the bottom.
images.caption: Four men playing pachisi, the Indian game that Ludo was adapted from: a watercolour painted in India, probably in 1851
images.credit: William Carpenter, probably 1851. Victoria and Albert Museum, via Wikimedia Commons

images.alt: Painted game board on cloth: a grid of numbered squares labelled in Devanagari script, with long dark snakes winding down across it and thin pale ladders leading upwards. Above the grid is a pavilion with seated crowned figures, flags and peacocks, a crowned rider on a deer to the left and a rider on a horse to the right.
images.caption: A Jain snakes-and-ladders board called gyan bazi, painted in gouache on cloth, India, 19th century
images.credit: Unknown Jain artist, 19th century (date as given by the source). Via Wikimedia Commons
images.note: Provenance is thin: the Commons file cites only the website herenow4u.net, with no holding museum, and the 19th-century date comes from that description. Better-documented boards found were not public domain (Wellcome Collection boards are CC BY 4.0; V&A images are non-commercial only).

images.alt: Oil painting of a young girl in a red bonnet, red checked dress and blue apron standing in the snow. She holds a school slate with books on it in one arm and a basket of red-and-white striped cloth on the other, with snowy village roofs behind her.
images.caption: A Swiss schoolgirl with her slate, books and sewing basket, painted by Albert Anker in 1878
images.credit: Albert Anker, 1878. Kunstmuseum Bern, via Wikimedia Commons

images.alt: Photograph of a wooden box with a clear plastic top full of wires and relays. Its front panel is labelled Nimwit, with Player wins and Machine wins signs, four columns of small lamps, four black buttons and two dials.
images.caption: Nimwit, a Nim-playing machine built by the mathematician Claude Shannon around 1953, now in the MIT Museum
images.credit: Photograph by Daderot, 2026, of an object in the MIT Museum, via Wikimedia Commons
images.note: A recent photograph of a real machine from about 1953, not a period photograph. No public-domain photograph of the 1940 Nimatron or the 1951 Nimrod was found: Commons has only a 479 x 901 px Nimatron patent drawing and CC BY-SA photos of a modern Nimrod replica in Berlin, and the Bouton portrait there is 322 x 486 px.

images.alt: Black-and-white photograph of a long single-file line of people bent under heavy packs, climbing a steep snow slope towards a mountain pass, with more people, sleds and piles of supplies at the bottom.
images.caption: Gold seekers climbing the snowy Chilkoot Pass on the way to the Klondike gold fields, Alaska, 1898
images.credit: Eric A. Hegg, 1898. Library of Congress, via Wikimedia Commons

images.alt: Black-and-white photograph of a small girl in a frilly white dress and bonnet holding two sticks joined by a string, with a diabolo spool on the ground at her feet. Empty wooden grandstands rise on the right and a man in white stands blurred in the background.
images.caption: A young girl playing diabolo, France, 1907, at the height of the diabolo craze
images.credit: Agence Rol, 1907. Bibliothèque nationale de France, via Wikimedia Commons

images.alt: An old hand-coloured map of Europe mounted on wood and cut into pieces along the borders of the countries. A few pieces are missing, leaving dark gaps where Scotland, the Netherlands and some islands should be. A decorated title in the corner reads Europe divided into its kingdoms, 1766.
images.caption: John Spilsbury's map of Europe cut into pieces along the borders, one of the first jigsaw puzzles, London, 1766
images.credit: John Spilsbury, 1766. British Library, via Wikimedia Commons

images.alt: Colour woodblock print of three kabuki actors in brightly patterned robes. Two crouch side by side at the front, holding out their hands in game gestures, while the third leans over behind them with his hands at his mouth, watching. The upper half of the print is filled with small grey figures showing the poses of the game, with lines of Japanese writing between them and a large title in black.
images.caption: Kabuki actors playing a ken hand game, a Japanese relative of rock-paper-scissors: woodblock print titled Hatsuuma tanuki-ken, Japan, 1861
images.credit: Utagawa Yoshitsuya, 1861. National Diet Library, Japan, via Wikimedia Commons
images.note: Title on the print and on Commons: 初午狸拳 (Hatsuuma tanuki-ken). Commons structured data tags it as kitsune-ken, but the printed title names tanuki-ken, so the caption uses the general term ken.

images.alt: Black-and-white photograph of a very old man with white hair and a beard, in a dark suit and tie, sitting at a small table and filling in a newspaper crossword with a pencil, with a thick dictionary propped open beside him.
images.caption: Ambrose Hines of Washington, D.C., who had just turned 100, solving a newspaper crossword during the crossword craze, 1925
images.credit: Harris & Ewing, 1925. Library of Congress, via Wikimedia Commons
images.note: Shows the 1924-25 crossword craze, not the 1913 puzzle. No scan of the original 21 December 1913 New York World page was found on Commons or the Internet Archive; the only Commons image (File:First_crossword.png) is a modern 300 x 615 px re-creation, and File:Arthurwynne.jpg shows a different Arthur Wynne (a British general), so neither was used. The Library of Congress catalogue truncates the sitter's surname as Hin[...]; the visible title reads Mr. Hines.

images.alt: Black-and-white photograph of a huge grey warship at anchor, seen from close to the bow, with two tall masts, three funnels and a long gun barrel pointing forward. A ladder runs down her side to a small boat, and the words H.M.A.S. Australia are written along the bottom of the picture.
images.caption: The battlecruiser HMAS Australia, the Royal Australian Navy's first flagship, which was commissioned in 1913
images.credit: Bain News Service, date unknown. Library of Congress, via Wikimedia Commons
images.note: The Library of Congress record dates this negative 1910, which cannot be right because the ship was launched in 1911, so the date is given as unknown. A Sydney alternative, thought to show her arrival in Sydney Harbour in October 1913, is File:HMAS_AUSTRALIA_I_in_Farm_Cove,_Sydney.jpg (Samuel J. Hood Studio, Australian National Maritime Museum, no known copyright restrictions, 3208 px); it is less dramatic at banner size.
